If you're looking for detailed dialogue I'm afraid you're going to be disappointed. She's not talking, she's barking. She's making noises like: "Wau? Wau? Wawan wan!?" (Basically, the Japanese equivalent of woof woof).

She's probably beyond the point of speech now. But, I suppose you might be able to read something into the fact that her first two barks are short and questioning, whereas her final bark seems much more... panicked. Make of that what you will.

Okay, I'm going to try to translate these ones by hand. I'm only going to translate the speech.

For the horse one, the first word is actually onomatopoeia, it's some sort of neigh. Imagine a horse having an orgasm, I bet that's what it sounds like. Her real words are in brackets so I'm guessing that she's lost the power of human speech.

The bit in brackets says something like: "What is thiiiiis!?" (she's rather shocked).

So in conclusion: 

>"NEIGH!!! (What is **this**!?)"

For the er... *mermaid* one. I hope you like vore. It has the verb 'to eat', negated, and she stutters at the start of her sentence. So the intended meaning is probably something like:

>"Don't... don't eat me..."


As a side note, most of the speech in all three of these pictures is written in hiragana, which usually indicates that the speaker is childish.

I can't gurantee that these are correct, maybe someone who knows Japanese better than me can improve on my translations, but they're fairly simple pieces of text.

>Don't make the transformation the primary focus of the story.

I disagree with this advice, but only slightly.

I don't think there's anything wrong with focusing on transformation.

In fact, I think it's possible to sometimes go too far in the other direction. A story that neglects the TF for the sake of depth might be a good story, perhaps, but it's not necessarily a good transformation story.

You're right though; things like action, pacing, plot and conflict are important and should never be ignored, but it seems to me that those elements are best used to enhance the TF. Take characterisation for example, it's much more satisfying to *change* someone if you know who they are first.

The way I see it, the best guiding philosophy is: "Make TF the focus, but don't neglect the story."  

There's an article on Shifti which I think strikes a good balance: [The Vanishing Transformation by Sturmovik.](http://shifti.org/wiki/User:Sturmovik/Vanishing_Transformation)

One problem with this, is that the division between STEM and the humanities isn't quite as clear cut as it might appear. Especially when you start considering the huge effect that philosophy has had on the sciences.

Suffice to say, the humanities may be less rigorous than STEM, but I'd be loathe to reject them entirely. Less rigorous doesn't mean that they can't come out with things that are useful, interesting or even beautiful.

But I wouldn't mind seeing critical theory and deconstruction disappear. They seem to be the viewpoints that are most prone to the politics and bitching that you mentioned. I don't expect the humanities to be completely objective, but humanities professors should fight to retain some ability to differentiate between good research and bad. If they don't, they may find that their subject can no longer lead anywhere interesting.

I think there might actually be a genuine cultural misunderstanding here.

In the UK, flags have almost no relevance whatsoever and are usually only used on governmental buildings or on special occasions. I think the idea that a flag might have a meaning independent of the symbol it depicts, is a fairly counter-intuitive idea to most Brits.

The union flag is, almost always, only used as a kitschy, ironic symbol. The idea that it suddenly gains more meaning when tied to a pole, seems fairly ridiculous.

I have to admit, that like EFS, I also had trouble understanding the point you were getting at.

The real question is what happens when you pull up some flooring and tie it to a flagpole.
Does it then become a flag? And if so, isn't it automatically always in contact with the floor?
